lessons.title: Cost and speed
lessons.summary: Tokens, latency and making AI affordable at scale.

cards.title: Pricing by tokens

viz.f: cost = in tokens × in price + out tokens × out price

cards.text: APIs charge per million input and output tokens. Output tokens usually cost several times more than input tokens, and larger models cost much more than small ones.

deep.x: Model APIs price usage per million tokens, with separate rates for input and output. Prices vary by model tier, provider, region and features like caching or batch processing.

v.f: cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price

deep.x: Why output costs more
Input tokens are processed in parallel in one pass; output tokens are generated one at a time, each requiring a full pass through the model, so they use more compute per token.
Price tiers

v.unit: price per million output tokens, $ (illustrative tiers)

deep.x: Other charges
Many providers offer free tiers or credits for experimentation, but production use needs proper budgeting.

cards.title: A worked example
cards.text: 10,000 requests a day, each with 2,000 input and 300 output tokens. At $3 per million input and $15 per million output tokens: $60 + $45 = $105 per day.

deep.x: Estimating costs early avoids surprises. Start from volumes and token counts per request.
Sensitivity
Hidden multipliers

x: Retries after errors or validation failures
Agent loops calling the model many times per task

deep.x: Budget controls
Always estimate at expected peak volume, not pilot volume.

cards.title: Latency
cards.text: Users feel two delays: time to first token (how long before text starts) and generation speed (tokens per second). Streaming the answer makes waiting feel shorter.

deep.x: Two latency measures shape user experience: time to first token (TTFT), and output speed in tokens per second.
What drives latency
Example

x: Total ≈ 5.5 s, but text appears after 0.5 s

deep.x: Reducing latency
Reasoning models
Thinking time can add seconds to minutes before an answer starts. Show progress indicators or use them asynchronously.
Users perceive streamed answers as faster even when total time is the same, because they can start reading immediately.

cards.title: Use the smallest capable model
cards.text: Small models can be 10–50 times cheaper than the largest ones. Route simple tasks to them and reserve big models for hard cases.

deep.x: The cheapest model that meets quality requirements should handle each task. Many tasks don't need frontier intelligence.
Task fit
Cascades
A cascade tries a cheap model first and escalates to a larger one only if confidence is low or validation fails.
Distillation
For very high-volume tasks, fine-tuning a small model on a large model's outputs can deliver large-model quality at small-model prices.
Measure quality per tier on your eval set; the cheapest acceptable tier usually wins.

cards.title: Shorten the prompt
cards.text: Trim instructions, retrieve fewer but better passages and avoid resending unchanged context. Every token saved is saved on every request.

deep.x: Input tokens are multiplied by every request. Small savings per request add up at scale.
Example savings
Don't cut clarity
Removing context the model needs causes errors and retries that cost more. Test quality after trimming.
Structured outputs save tokens
Asking for JSON with defined fields avoids verbose prose when software is the consumer.
Tool and function definitions count as input tokens on every call; agents with dozens of tools carry a hidden token overhead.

cards.title: Caching
cards.text: Cache repeated prompts (prompt caching) and repeated answers (response caching). FAQ-type questions can often be answered from a cache.

deep.x: Two kinds of caching cut cost and latency: prompt caching at the provider and response caching in your application.

items: reuses whole answers to identical or similar questions

deep.x: Prompt caching
Put stable content (instructions, reference documents, tool definitions) at the start of prompts. Providers cache it for minutes to hours and charge a fraction for reuse.
Response caching
For FAQs or repeated queries, store answers and serve them directly. Semantic caching matches questions with similar meaning using embeddings.
Cautions

items: Expire cached answers when sources change
Don't cache personalised or sensitive answers inappropriately

deep.x: Caching is often the single biggest cost lever for high-traffic assistants.

cards.title: Batch processing
cards.text: For work that isn't urgent, such as classifying a backlog of documents overnight, batch APIs offer large discounts (often around half price) in exchange for slower turnaround.

deep.x: Batch APIs process large sets of requests asynchronously, typically within 24 hours, at roughly half the normal price.
Good candidates
Workflow
Combining discounts
Batch processing can combine with prompt caching for further savings on repetitive workloads.
Overnight batch jobs let teams process years of archived documents for a modest one-off cost.

cards.title: Reasoning costs
cards.text: Reasoning models generate many "thinking" tokens before answering. They're more accurate on hard tasks but slower and more expensive, so use them where the extra quality matters.

deep.x: Reasoning models generate hidden "thinking" tokens before the visible answer, billed as output tokens. A short visible answer might involve thousands of reasoning tokens.
When it's worth it
Effort controls
Many providers let you set reasoning effort or thinking budgets, balancing accuracy against cost and latency.
Measure
Compare cost per correct answer, not cost per request: if a reasoning model solves a task first time where a cheaper model needs three attempts and human fixes, it may be cheaper overall.
Use reasoning selectively, routed to the tasks that need it.

cards.title: Measure cost per outcome
cards.text: Track cost per resolved ticket, per processed invoice or per report, not just per token. A pricier model that needs fewer retries and corrections can be cheaper overall.

deep.x: Token prices are inputs; business value is measured per outcome: resolved tickets, processed invoices, completed reports.

v.f: cost per outcome = (model + infrastructure + human review) ÷ successful outcomes

deep.x: Example
Full picture
Comparing with the baseline
If an invoice used to take 6 minutes of staff time and now takes 1 minute of review plus €0.05 of AI, the saving is clear even with premium models.
Optimising for cheapest tokens can increase total cost if quality drops and humans must fix more.

cards.title: Prices keep falling
cards.text: The price for a given level of capability has dropped dramatically year after year. Plans that look too costly today may be affordable next year.

deep.x: The cost of a given capability level has fallen dramatically, driven by better hardware, efficient models, competition and inference optimisations.

items: Revisit use cases rejected as too costly
Avoid long fixed-price commitments without review

deep.x: Jevons paradox
As AI gets cheaper per task, organisations use it for more tasks, so total spend often rises even as unit costs fall.
Frontier stays expensive
While old capability levels get cheap, the newest, most capable models remain premium-priced.
Plan for falling unit prices and rising usage at the same time.

lessons.title: Risks and responsible use
lessons.summary: Misuse, bias, IP and keeping people safe.

cards.title: A map of risks
cards.text: Risks include wrong answers, biased outputs, leaking confidential data, copyright issues, deepfakes and fraud, misuse for harmful purposes, and over-reliance by users.

deep.x: Generative AI risks span technical, legal, ethical and organisational dimensions. Frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023) and ISO/IEC 42001 (2023) help organise them.
Likelihood and impact
Risk management cycle
Proportionality
Controls should match risk: lightweight for internal brainstorming, rigorous for customer-facing or decision-making systems.
A use-case inventory with risk ratings is the foundation of AI governance.

cards.title: Data leakage
cards.text: Pasting confidential data into consumer AI tools may send it outside your organisation. Use approved enterprise tools that don't train on your data and meet your security requirements.

deep.x: Data leakage happens when confidential or personal information reaches places it shouldn't: external providers without agreements, other users, logs or model training.

items: data may be retained or used per consumer terms

deep.x: Incidents
In 2023 Samsung engineers reportedly pasted confidential source code into a public chatbot, leading the company to restrict such tools.
Leakage paths
Controls
Banning AI tools outright often drives usage underground; providing safe approved tools is more effective.

cards.title: Bias

items: Human review for decisions about people

cards.text: Models reflect patterns in their training data and can produce stereotyped or unequal outputs. Test outputs across groups for uses affecting people, like hiring or credit.

deep.x: Generative models can reproduce stereotypes: assuming professions' genders, under-representing groups in images, or treating dialects and names differently.

items: Different tone by names or dialects

deep.x: Testing

steps: Create matched prompts varying only group attributes

deep.x: High-stakes uses
Using generative AI to screen CVs, assess employees or evaluate creditworthiness falls into high-risk categories under the EU AI Act, requiring rigorous bias testing and oversight.
Mitigations
Test with the people your system will serve, in the languages they use.

cards.title: Intellectual property
cards.text: Questions remain about training on copyrighted works and owning AI outputs. Check that generated text or code doesn't reproduce protected material, and follow your company's policy.

deep.x: IP risks run both ways: outputs may infringe others' rights, and your inputs may expose your own IP.

items.b: generated text or code resembling protected works

deep.x: Code assistants
Some coding tools offer filters that block suggestions matching public code, and vendors may offer indemnities against copyright claims.

items: Keep human authorship in key work
Document AI use for important assets

deep.x: Copyright of outputs

items: publishing AI output that mirrors a known work

deep.x: Several major AI providers offer enterprise customers legal indemnity for copyright claims arising from model outputs, under conditions.

cards.title: Over-reliance
cards.text: People tend to trust fluent, confident AI too much, a form of automation bias. Keep humans engaged and accountable, especially for important decisions.

deep.x: Automation bias leads people to accept AI outputs without enough scrutiny, especially when they're fluent, fast and usually right.
Evidence

A 2023 Harvard–BCG study found consultants using AI performed much better on tasks within AI's capabilities, but were more likely to get wrong answers on a task just outside them, trusting flawed outputs.

Relying on AI for tasks you never learn can leave you unable to spot errors. Deliberate practice and understanding remain important.

items: Require brief human reasoning for key decisions
Train staff on AI failure modes

deep.x: The "jagged frontier": AI is excellent at some tasks and poor at similar-looking ones; know where the edges are.

cards.title: Misuse safeguards

deep.x: Model providers apply layered safeguards against misuse: training models to refuse harmful requests, classifiers detecting dangerous content, usage policies and abuse monitoring.
Priority risks
Jailbreaks
Users try role-play, encoding and multi-step tricks to bypass refusals. Providers patch vulnerabilities and run bug bounties; it's an ongoing contest.
Balance
Good safeguards minimise both harm and unnecessary refusals, allowing legitimate medical, security and research questions while blocking real uplift for attackers.
Providers report regularly on misuse they've detected and disrupted, such as influence operations and scam networks.

cards.title: Transparency
cards.text: Tell people when they're interacting with AI or reading AI-generated content where it matters. The EU AI Act requires this for chatbots and deepfakes.

deep.x: Transparency about AI use supports trust, informed choice and accountability.

items.b: document AI involvement in key work

deep.x: Legal requirements
The EU AI Act requires informing people they're interacting with an AI system (unless obvious), and labelling deepfakes and certain AI-generated public-interest text.
Practical approaches
When disclosure matters most
Honest disclosure rarely hurts trust; discovering undisclosed AI use often does.

cards.title: Environmental footprint
cards.text: Training and running large models use significant electricity and water for cooling. Efficient models, right-sizing and clean energy reduce the footprint.

deep.x: Generative AI uses energy for training and, increasingly, for inference at massive scale, plus water for cooling data centres and resources for chips.
Context
Estimates per request have fallen as hardware and models improve; recent provider disclosures put a typical text query at fractions of a watt-hour. Total demand still grows with usage.
Reducing footprint

deep.x: Corporate reporting

cards.title: Policies at work

cards.title: Start with your bottlenecks

Track your time

Start small
Pick one workflow, refine it until it works reliably, then expand.

cards.title: Learn faster

cards.title: Analyse data

Review for anything that doesn't sound like you

cards.title: Prepare for meetings

deep.x: AI can turn scattered documents into a focused briefing and turn meetings into clear outcomes.
Before the meeting
After the meeting
Negotiations

Custom assistants
Organising knowledge
Keep key reference documents (style guides, product facts, glossaries) ready to attach, so assistants work from accurate context.

Human connection
Condolence messages, difficult feedback and personal apologies carry weight because they come from you. AI can help you think, but the words should be yours.

People report AI is most useful for tasks they already know well enough to judge the result.

Habits

Keep a log of useful prompts
Follow a couple of trusted sources

deep.x: Measuring your progress
Team learning
